**How each pull stays weak and easy to ignore**
- **Prior:** a bounded learnable weight times tanh(gold at stake / 5,000). It starts at 0.5, so no pull adds more than half a logit at the start, and it can fall to 0 or rise to 2.
- **Feature:** read through weights that start at zero, so it changes nothing until learning finds a use for it.

**The chains**
- **Week start → main hero goes home:** a main hero is pulled toward one of our towns by what the town can give it: its garrison, plus as much of its army for hire as our gold buys. This applies to tiles in reach (MOVE) and to map areas (TRAVEL). No week rule was needed: the value is highest at the week start anyway, because that's when new creatures appear.
- **A threat → go home, buy defenders:** any hero is pulled toward a threatened town of ours, by the danger times what the town is worth (buildings and garrison). "Recruit straight into the hero" also fades as the town's danger rises, so defenders stay in the garrison.
- **Scouts ferry troops:** a scout carrying troops is pulled toward the main hero. When they meet, the existing hand-over prior moves the troops to the stronger hero.
- **Hiring:** NK2's rule lifts HIRE: no hero yet, lots of treasure per hero, a threat or gold to spare, or gold piling up. Its weight falls as we have more heroes.
- **Trade → build:** VCMI's own "buildable but for resources" state is now a raw input (campaign contract v6). Torch works out what those buildings lack and what we have beyond their needs, and lifts trades that buy one with the other.

**Kill a guard, take what it blocks**

I built it. I don't think it's easy to learn without it: a guard with nothing on its own tile looks like a pure loss, so the policy would rarely attack it and never discover the artifact behind it. Now a wandering monster's fight is credited with half the best object in a pocket you can reach only through its guarded zone, times the chance of winning. The half is learnable from 0 to 1. Your case is covered: a great artifact behind a beatable guard now pulls the hero to fight for it, and a guard you'd lose to still doesn't.

[2026-10-28 23:06] AI: Yes, we need an end-of-game head, and it should drive the policy, not just serve as a test. I've built it, together with the two pieces it depends on. 239 tests pass, and a real 30-day game plus one update ran clean (9.5 s, 1.94 MB of records, 12.3 MB/min). The end value was known for every decision, and nothing is left running. Nothing is committed.

## What's built

- **Random game ends.** Each training game now ends on day 28 plus a random number of days, averaging 28 more, with a hard stop at day 112.
  - After day 28, every day is equally likely to be the last, and the AI never sees the cap.
  - This matters: with a fixed day-56 end, an end-of-game head would learn to game the cutoff ("don't build on day 54").
  - Average length is about 54 days, so throughput is about the same as now. About 5% of games run to day 112, so I raised the per-game time limit from 360 s to 600 s. Evaluations stay at day 56.
- **The end head (V_end).** It predicts the player's share at the game's end and replaces my 14-day helper head.
  - It is graded against its own forecast at the player's next day, mixed with the real end. The more the head is trusted, the more weight its forecast gets; at least 25% stays the real end.
  - A player knocked out ends with 0. A game cut short by the time limit has no end value.
- **The automatic switch** (your "use it late in training"). The policy's credit is `(1−b)` × the 7-day credit + `b` × the end credit, where `b` rises as V_end proves it predicts the end.
  - The end credit compares V_end at the next decision with V_end now, plus 25% from V_end a week later. It deliberately uses no whole-game outcome, because a whole game's luck would drown the signal; V_end learns from the real end, and the credit gets it through V_end.
  - Decisions in the last week before a cap used to get no credit at all, because there's no share 7 days on; they now get the end credit.
  - `campaign.end_credit_max=0` keeps V_end for testing only.

No hand-made bias. I agree with you: it would fix only the cases we know about.

## A flaw I found and fixed

The 7-day heads' "trust" (the score that decides how much the credit leans on them) gave them about 0.3 for free at the start, before they had learned anything. The player count alone predicts much of a share (½ in 2-player games, ¼ in 4-player), and the heads start at that guess. That alone made them about 75% trusted, by my estimate. Trust is now measured as how much better they do than the player-count guess, for V2/V5/V7 and V_end. As a result, early training leans on real outcomes for longer: slower to start, but honest.

## What we need before training

1. **War machines at half price.** You decided this, but it isn't built in this tree: the empire value still counts them as 0 and the battle reward ignores them. It changes both rewards, so it has to go in before the run. I recommend I build it next.
2. **Re-run both value audits** after step 1.
3. **A 20–30 minute full-power dry run** of the actual joint training setup. It should measure throughput, how many long games hit the 600 s limit, update time and MB/min.

## What can wait

- **The battle weight-migration batch** (mana price, spell cost, stake, summoned units' worth, obstacle kind, HEAL/CATAPULT heads, tactics order out of C++). None of it is a reward bug: summoned units and clones are already excluded from what a side keeps. I recommend applying it as one migration at the first campaign restart; there will be one.
- **Past-version opponents in campaign games.** Build them only if the evaluations against Nullkiller2 stall or the version-to-version score keeps going negative.
- **The deferred list stays deferred:** TRAVEL guards/enemy reach, per-hero visits, moving `castValue`'s gold pricing to torch, C++ mask tests, and the remaining Nullkiller2 pieces.

## What we may have missed

- **Long horizon doesn't solve exploration.** V_end values Wisdom only under the current policy. If the policy never builds Mage Guild 3+ and visits it, Wisdom is worth nothing to it, at any horizon. Only Nullkiller2's skill and building priors and the entropy floor seed it. I added a TensorBoard metric for exactly your worry, `campaign_skills/<skill>`, the pick rate when a skill is offered. Watch Estates against Wisdom, Offence and Earth Magic.
- **Mispricing becomes exploitable on any day.** V_end maximizes the share at an end that can come on any day after 28, so any mistake in how the empire value prices something can be exploited at any time. That's why the audits matter after the war-machine change.
- **The switch may stop partway.** Watch `head_ev_vend` and `end_credit` in `progress.csv`. If V_end's score plateaus below 0.4, the credit stays a partial mix by design. Lower `trust_full_ev` only if V_end's predictions look good.

1. **Battle reward:** VCMI's casualties include destroyed war machines, which no army's starting value counted. So a destroyed ballista cost its side 2500 that it never had.

6. **Lost games:** one damaged records message threw away the whole game; now only that message is skipped.
7. **Value-head trust:** two estimator flaws.
   - Plain explained variance credited the heads for the player count alone, giving them ~0.3 for free.
   - Averaging per-update ratios let a single 4-game update swing it from +0.4 to −1.0.

   Trust now uses explained variance over the 1/players prior, with its two variances pooled across updates.

[2026-10-29 07:56] AI: Here's why the battle model stopped shooting while its score stayed flat. The cause is real, and it's the same underlying problem joint1 had.

**1. The score stayed flat because 3201 really got better elsewhere.** On the same 200 eval battles, 3201 beats 3078 by +0.016 ± 0.007 (about 2σ):

| Set | 3201 minus 3078 |
|---|---|
| Sieges | +0.030 ± 0.017 |
| Generated | +0.039 ± 0.025 |
| Hard | +0.014 ± 0.012 |
| The 7 battles where it idled more | −0.030 each |

The idle rate also overstates how widespread the problem is. 3201's 43 idle turns come from just those 7 battles, one of them the long Zombie fight. On 315 fixed states with a full-damage shot available, SHOOT stops being the top choice in 15% of them at 2840 and 20–23% at 3201, and many of those alternatives are melee or a spell, not idling.

**2. Why the policy drifts: the battle policy's learning signal is noise.** The gradient study at 3078 measured each loss term's average effect on log p(SHOOT) per training step:

| Term | Generated battles | Campaign battles |
|---|---|---|
| Policy gradient | +47 (t 0.5; minibatch agreement 0.18, pure noise is 0.20) | −139 (t −2.0) |
| Entropy floor | −2.8 (t −5.8) | −3.0 (t −8.8) |
| Value loss | +0.7 (t +3.9) | +1.7 (t +7.7) |

- The policy gradient is a random walk. Some steps happen to help sieges, some happen to erode shooting, which is why the total is flat while behaviour wanders.
- On top of that walk, one term pushes away from shooting every single update: the entropy floor I introduced in B1. It raises the entropy of every decision below 0.3 nats, including a shot that is 99% certain. That erodes near-certain shots until the noise flips the borderline ones to waiting or moving.
- The campaign battles' policy push (t −2) is borderline and doesn't come from the credit. In campaign battles, shots get higher advantages than not shooting (+0.050 vs +0.018 for MOVE).
- The value loss now pushes slightly toward shooting, the opposite of joint1.

**What I'd do (the battle model stays frozen at 3078 until you decide):**
1. **Stop the floor from eroding confident correct actions.** Either lower it to ~0.1 nats, or apply it only to the action-type choice where the top two types are close. This is a small change.
2. **The real fix is signal, not regularizers.** The battle credit carries almost no per-decision information; joint1's study found the same. That needs a credit or value redesign: your call.
3. **Keep 3078 frozen rather than 3201 for now.** 3201's +0.016 is only 2σ and comes bundled with a known dumb behaviour. Resuming training without fix 1 would just walk on.

Separately, the campaign is now improving for real. The update-104 eval against Nullkiller2 scored 0.244, which is +0.120 ± 0.050 over the first eval (~2.4σ), with 16 eliminations.

I think so, at least in part. The flat score and the drift have different causes, and the drift is the real problem. Everything below comes from joint2's logs, TensorBoard and checkpoints. I ran no battles and didn't touch the other thread's processes.

Why the score stayed flat: those shots were worth almost nothing under our reward

- The reward only counts what's left at the end.
  - When you win, the enemy's whole army counts as lost whether you shot it or not. A shot only pays through the losses it prevents, and waiting, kiting and defending prevent losses too.
  - When you lose, only the damage you dealt counts.
- The value head has learned exactly that. The training log fits how V moves against our losses and our kills:
  - For the attacker (wins 70% of evals), V moves −0.43 per share of our army lost, but only +0.10 to +0.24 per share of the enemy's killed.
  - For the defender, who usually loses, it's the reverse.
  - Cyclops kiting and Archers defending are what "don't get hit" looks like.
- The evals agree.
  - 2840 (4% idle) and 3201 (31% idle) score the same: +0.077 and +0.078.
  - Army kept and army killed are unchanged on both sides.
  - On the same battles, two models' scores differ with an SE of ~0.005, so the skipped shots cost less than ~0.01.
- I don't think something else got really good. Nothing improved by more than the normal jitter between evals.
- It has happened before. In v14-11h, shooters went from 90% to 55% shooting "while the outcomes stayed the same" (the comment in distributions.py:entropy).

Why it drifts: nothing holds shooting up, so any steady push wins

- The training signal for shooting is noise. The 2026-10-28 gradient study measured it at noise level, for the reason above. This is the third drift: v14-11h, joint1 (the entropy bonus), and now joint2.
- The entropy floor (B1) may have moved the push rather than removed it. Not verified yet.
  - The floor's weight is 10x the old bonus (0.1 vs 0.01), but it applies only to decisions sharper than 0.3 nats.
  - The sharpest decisions that aren't forced are probably confident single-target shots. So the floor's whole push would land on p(SHOOT): it pushes them down to about 0.95, and through shared weights on every shooting state.
  - The share of decisions below the floor rose from 4.9% to 8.5% during the run.
- The other candidate is the value loss, which pushes through the shared trunk. It was measured at t ≈ −5 on p(SHOOT) in joint1, and B1 didn't touch it.
  - A possible route, also unverified: SHOOT's type logit includes the best target's score (best_of). The target softmax never pins that score's level. So a trunk change can move p(SHOOT), and only the noisy type gradient pushes back.
- The other thread's study will tell which. Its gradient study already has both the floor and value terms, so the run on 3078 will settle it.

The weight average (B3) makes the drift look worse than it is

- In all 5 evals, the averaged weights scored below the live ones on the same battles. Pooled: −0.0075 ± 0.0025.
- At 3315 the average idles 0.25 against BattleAI and 0.49 against MMAI; the live weights idle 0.15.
- So the real drift is 0.03 → 0.15, not → 0.49. B3 didn't work. I'd evaluate the live weights until we know why.

What I'd check, then do

1. In the paired 3078/3201 run, split the idle turns by whether that side won. I expect them to cost about nothing where it won and something where it lost.
2. Count the decisions below the floor by action type. If most are SHOOT, set entropy_floor_weight=0; PPO's 20% clip already limits how fast a choice can sharpen.
3. If the value loss turns out to be the push, cut its gradient into the inputs the action heads read.
4. The root problem stays either way: the reward says nothing about these shots. If you want 0.99 shooting, something has to make them count:
   - a fixed prior on SHOOT when a full-damage shot is legal, using the same fixed-prior-plus-learned-correction pattern as the other priors;
   - or a lower-variance target, i.e. search.

   Otherwise the next steady push will move it again, in places where we have no metric to notice.

I added these findings to the plan memory, with the floor explanation marked as unverified.

[2026-10-29 15:41] AI: I fixed the idle-shooter metric, and joint2 is running again with it (battle from epoch 3873, campaign from update 158). Even on the stricter definition, shooters still skip a full-damage shot 21% of the time.

The old metric already ignored a WAIT followed by a full-damage shot, because it judged the whole round. But it had two flaws. After a WAIT the shot could disappear (an enemy steps next to the shooter or out of range), and the forced DEFEND still counted. And it counted kiting as idle.

**New definition** (`shooter_not_shooting`, per decision):
- **Counts:** a decision that ends the shooter's turn while a full-damage shot is legal right then, if it DEFENDs or MOVEs without escaping melee.
- **Never counts:** a WAIT, including the decision after one if the shot is gone by then.
- **Doesn't count:** a MOVE off a hex that enemy melee could reach next turn, to a hex reachable by less of the enemy army (kiting). At 3792, 38% of the "idle" moves were this.

On the same 200 eval battles at 3792 (no randomness), it reads **0.21** against BattleAI, versus 0.33 on the old definition. In TensorBoard the eval and training curves will drop at this restart because of the new definition, not the model.

**A real bug was killing 30–60% of campaign games, and it's fixed.** These games were being killed by the 60-second no-output watchdog. The cause was battles that never ended: 1,000+ decisions per side, almost all DEFEND and MOVE. At about 0.4 MB of record per decision, sending the record then blocked for over a minute. A killed game sends no record, so the model never trained on its own stalemates. There were two sources:
- **Our model played the wandering monsters.** Monsters can't flee, so the existing retreat rule (after 30 rounds without damage) could never end their battles. Monsters are now played by BattleAI, as in a real game, both in campaign games and in generated monster battles.

**Campaign score: no, it's not −1 to 1.** In each eval game, our model takes one seat and Nullkiller2 the others, on 2-, 3- and 4-player maps. The score is our share of the total empire value at day 56, multiplied by the number of players, then averaged over 24 games:
- **0** means we were eliminated.
- **1** means we have as much as the average player in that game.
- **The maximum** is the number of players (2, 3 or 4), meaning we own everything.

So 0.227 means our empire is about a quarter of an average player's. In a 2-player game that's about 11% of the total. We're eliminated in 18 of the 24 games, which score 0, so most of the mean comes from the 6 games we survive.

One related issue: the campaign eval samples moves at temperature 1, not greedily like the battle evals. That's part of why its error bar is so wide (±0.09). Greedy play would make it less noisy, but it risks the model repeating the same move forever, so I haven't changed it.

**Value loss: `eval/battle_value_loss` and `eval/campaign_value_loss`**
- **How it's measured:** each update's decisions are scored by the model before it trains on them, with every value head weighted as the training loss weights them.
- **What it subtracts:** the value loss is a cross-entropy, which can't go below the labels' own entropy, so I subtract that floor. A perfect V scores 0.
- **Why that matters:** the old `loss/value` was about 0.685 for battles, and almost all of that is label entropy (ln 2 ≈ 0.693 for an even battle). It mostly moved with how one-sided the battles were. The part V can actually reduce is about 0.006, roughly an RMS error of 0.11 in V on the −1 to 1 scale. That's the number that should go down.
- **Values so far:** battle 0.005–0.008 per epoch, campaign 0.0013 on its first update. Each point is one update, so turn on smoothing in TensorBoard.

[2026-10-29 20:29] AI: I added a round limit to VCMI itself, and it's live without stopping training: every game started from now on uses the new build.

**The rule:** at round 60 the attacker retreats, using VCMI's normal retreat (it loses its army and keeps its hero). If the attacker can't retreat, the defender does. If neither can, the battle continues and the engine logs a warning. Our AI's own rules still act first, at rounds 50 and 55, so the engine limit only catches what they can't: a side with no hero that keeps out of reach of an attacker like BattleAI, which never retreats.

**Why the attacker gives up:** in a real game, retreat is the attacker's only way out of a fight it can't finish. VCMI's retreat path is also the one already tested, so nothing else in the game's bookkeeping changes. The cost is that a defender with no hero that can't be caught now forces the attacker to lose its army. Training already works this way since this afternoon, when our side is ahead.

**Tested:** I added a `VCMI_BATTLE_ROUND_LIMIT` override for tests and played three battles with the limit at 2. All ended at round 2 with the attacker retreating, and our AI's records came through normally. The 250 Python tests pass.

**Pushed:** the engine patch is vcmi `d1a5f29bb`, labelled "not a bug fix", and main is at `47f2d64`. While I was working, the second machine had pushed Linux support and the `--machine` option to both repos, so I rebased my commits on top. Those changes are now in the working tree and the build. They're compatible with the running joint2: the `headless.sh` change falls back to the macOS `stat` command.

The watch list now tracks `campaign_eval/short`, which should stay at 0 from the next campaign eval on.

**Design problems that weaken learning, each needing your call:**
1. **The credit is mostly shared luck.** 72% of the advantage variance is common to all of a player's decisions on the same day (94% for the 7-day part), so it can't say which action helped. One action type (ARMY) failing the credit check, at t = −4.7, also shifts every type's credit to its noisiest part.

The same-state test shows BUILD isn't credited better than the alternatives. The drift comes from the state offsets in item 1 plus PPO's clipping, which favours the most likely action. The entropy floor doesn't protect this choice, because it counts the whole decision's entropy and the move table keeps that high.

**What changed** (pushed as `552625f`; time limits in `acd6999`):
- **Hiring:** the model now sees each tavern hero's experience, primary and secondary skills, army and artifacts (spellbook and war machines included). This is a contract change. A hire also gets its change to the empire value as a prior.

- **Campaign empire value:** heroes are valued by their skills.
  - The k-th primary point beyond a fresh hero's 5 is worth 400 × k; each secondary skill level is worth 2,000 (the University price); each level adds 200; experience toward the next level counts proportionally.
  - Only the strongest hero counts in full; the others count at 50%.
  - A fresh hero is worth 1,500, and the spellbook 500.
  - The ledger now sends base primary and secondary skills, and the in-graph value matches the ledger exactly.

**Measured effect:**
- In my test games, hires went from 0 to 8–14 per game.
- In self-play, heroes per player rose from 1.1–1.8 to 2.5.

**New problem: heroes die stepping next to strong monsters.** In three test games, 18 of 23 lost heroes died this way. A move onto a tile beside a monster starts a fight with it.
- The prior correctly rates those tiles as bad: −3,500 gold (median) on the fatal ones.

[2026-10-30 02:16] AI: While you were away I found two more things and fixed both. joint2 is training with them (pid 36437).

**1. The greedy campaign eval measured a broken mode, so I switched it back to sampling.** In greedy play, our heroes step back and forth one tile at a time until their movement runs out:
- With greedy play, 95% of moves were one tile, and 88% went back to a tile the hero already stood on that day.
- With sampled play, as in training, the same model makes 19% one-tile moves, and only 2% go back.

The move table spreads its probability over many distant targets, but its single best entry is often a neighbouring tile. Greedy chases that peak back and forth. So evals 310 and 321 understated the trained policy; treat them as unrepresentative. The campaign eval samples again; it's still seeded per game and seat, so paired comparisons still work. (`6008500`)

**2. Bad hires were never held back. Fixed.** The HIRE action type only got a boost when a hire was positive. A lone-creature hire, which loses about 1,500 of empire value, didn't push HIRE down at all. It now gets the hire's signed gain: in a quick check, a lone-creature hire's probability fell to 0.07 and a hire with a real army rose to 0.97. (`11e8254`)

**What the games against Nullkiller2 showed** (four eval-style games):
- **Broke:** gold stayed at 400–2,000 the whole game, and 10 hires (25,000 gold) went mostly on lone-creature heroes.
- **Heroes never reinforced:** they stood in our town in 19 of 3,611 decisions and never once moved troops between themselves and the town, though that was legal 18 times. All recruits went to the garrison.
- **Sitting targets:** our heroes stayed at level 2 and were killed on Nullkiller2's turns, while Nullkiller2's main hero reached level 10–15.
- **Early eliminations:** in both 3-player games we were eliminated by day 13–15.

The remaining big gap is that heroes never go home to collect troops. Self-play gives the model no pressure to learn that, since its opponents don't attack. That's where putting Nullkiller2 into training, or a "reinforce your main hero" prior, would help. Both are your call.

The next sampled campaign eval will be the new baseline for all of tonight's fixes.

[2026-10-30 09:21] AI: ## 1. Campaign model architecture

**Forward:** `campaign_model/model.py:841` (`CampaignModel.forward`).
- Hand-made features: `model.py:339` (`make_custom_features`), using `campaign_model/features.py`.
- Heads: `model.py:1046` (`outputs`).
- Inputs: `campaign_model/schema.py`, filled by `agents/AlphaMapAI/Encoder.cpp`.
- Size: token width 64, 32-channel tile features, 2 transformer layers, 4 heads.

The forward runs in four stages.

**Stage 1: hand-made features.** These are computed in the graph from raw inputs. Each prior has a few learnable corrections, kept within a range and pulled back by weight decay.
- **Φ:** its parts and total, equal to the ledger's.
- **Armies and heroes:** army strength and worth, hero worth, the gain from the next level.
- **Towns:** strength, value and danger.
- **Each tile in a hero's view:** its gold value, made of:
  - the object's worth (Nullkiller2 scores, `priors/object_values.csv`);
  - the fight's expected return (P(win) × gain − expected loss);
  - new land revealed;
  - the change in danger from enemy heroes.

  That value becomes the MOVE prior.
- **Each TRAVEL area:** its contents' worth, discounted by the days to reach it. This is the TRAVEL prior.
- **Nullkiller2's habits:** hero roles, skill scores at level-up, gold pressure, build rewards, upgrades, spellbook, hiring, trading.

**Stage 2: tokens.**
- **Global:** calendar, resources, income, the tavern's heroes, the question being asked, our previous decision, Φ.
- **Heroes** (ours, plus the other players' we can see): type, class and owner embeddings; numbers (level, primary skills, mana, movement, position); the sum of its stack embeddings; artifacts, skills, spells.
- **Towns:** faction and owner, numbers, built buildings, garrison stacks, and one recruit token per creature level, summed in.
- **Dialogs:** one token for the other army in an exchange, and up to 8 tokens for a question's options.
- **Hero window:** each of our heroes sees the 33×33 tiles around it. Tile embeddings go through two 3×3 convolutions and are pooled (mean and max) into that hero's token.
- **Whole map (`MapEncoder`):**
  - Every visible object is embedded onto a 36×36 grid per map level.
  - Convolutions reduce it to 18×18 (the TRAVEL areas) and then 9×9.
  - Each hero reads the 9×9 blocks by attention, biased by direction and distance (`MapReader`).
  - The global token gets their mean and max.

**Stage 3: trunk.** Two pre-norm transformer blocks over all tokens. Attention gets a bias from the tile distance between tokens that have a map position (heroes, towns, an option's object).

**Stage 4: heads.** Each head is a learned part plus its stage-1 prior.
- **Action type (12 types):** global token, a learned summary of what MOVE and TRAVEL offer, and couplings. Value left in reach holds back END and TRAVEL, and each action table's best prior pushes its own type.
- **MOVE:** the window's tile features are scaled and shifted by the hero token (FiLM). Each tile's logit adds its prior and a learned score of its features. The spell-target cell head reuses these tile features.
- **TRAVEL:** hero token matched against each area's features, plus a position MLP, the area's worth and the TRAVEL prior.
- **BUILD, RECRUIT, HIRE, ARMY, UPGRADE, TRADE, CAST, BUY, DISMISS:** small heads on the tokens involved, plus priors.
- **Question options:** each option token scored against the global token and the hero being asked about, plus Nullkiller2's skill scores.
- **Value:** an MLP on the global token, the mean of our hero and town tokens, and Φ. It outputs V2, V5 and V7 (our share 2, 5 and 7 days later), the growth heads and V_end (our share at the game's end).

**Where I'd look first:**
- The trunk is small next to the inputs, so most behaviour comes from the stage-1 priors.
- Tiles interact only through two 3×3 convolutions and the hero token.
- The MOVE prior prices an object by a fixed per-type table, not by what it gives this hero. An Arena is worth about 1,200 to a fresh main hero and over 5,000 to a level-10 one. A Temple is worth nothing to an undead army.

## 2. The value function (Φ)

**Your three examples:**
- **XP short of a level:** already counted since yesterday's version 2. Progress toward the next level counts pro rata at what that level-up brings. A Learning Stone's 1,000 XP is worth about 2,600 to a fresh main hero.
- **Primary skill points:** also counted since version 2. The k-th point beyond 5 is worth 400 × k for the main hero, half for others. Your formula does mean a School of War or Magic point (1,000 gold) loses value until the hero's 3rd extra point. Say if you want that changed.
- **Temporary luck/morale:** not counted. This one is a real gap.

I went through all the map object types in VCMI's config, plus the town buildings a visiting hero uses. Here is what Φ still ignores:

| What it gives | Where | Φ now |
|---|---|---|
| Spells | Shrines (3 levels), Pyramid, Scholar, mage guilds, Pandora's boxes and events | 0, apart from the mana cap |
| Luck/morale until the next battle | Buoy, Swan Pond, Faerie Ring, Fountains of Fortune and Youth, Idol, Mermaids, Oasis, Temple, Rally Flag, Watering Hole; Warrior's Tomb (−3 morale) | 0 |
| Movement | Stables (for the week); Oasis, Watering Hole, Rally Flag, Fountain of Youth (for the day); Swan Pond (costs the day's movement); Lighthouse | 0 |
| Puzzle map | Obelisks | 0, and we have no dig action, so the grail is out of reach anyway |
| Access, quests, information | Keymaster tents, Seer's Huts and Quest Guards (until they pay), Den of Thieves, signs | 0 |

Everything else is already counted: resources, XP, primary and secondary skills, artifacts, creatures, creature banks, mines, towns, prisons, map reveal (1 gold per tile) and mana up to its cap.

**Proposed version 3** (the numbers are my picks):
1. **Spells:** 500 × spell level for each spell in a hero's book, counted as part of its skills (strongest hero in full, others half).
   - Shrines would give 500, 1,000 and 1,500, a Pyramid 2,500.
   - A level-1 mage guild would give the main hero about 2,500.
2. **Luck and morale until the next battle.** In this game config each point is a 1/24 chance per stack of a double-damage hit or an extra turn. Bad morale costs 2/24 lost turns per point, and bad luck does nothing.
   - I'd price each 1/24 at 2% of the hero's army worth. That's about 4% more output in the next battle, of which roughly half shows in what the battle saves.
   - It counts only for stacks it affects (morale skips undead, non-living creatures and war machines) and stays within the ±3 caps.
   - With a 20k main army: Temple +400, Rally Flag +800, Warrior's Tomb −2,400.
3. **Movement:** leave it out. Φ is measured at the end of the day, after movement resets, and whatever the extra movement reaches is credited when it's picked up.
4. **Obelisks, keymasters, quests and information:** stay at 0, with the reason written in the list.
5. **The readable list:** a new `docs/empire_value.md` covering:
   - each kind of reward and its rule;
   - each object, what it gives, and what Φ adds.

   I'll also update `priors/object_values.csv`, whose MOVE-prior rows still say "Φ: none" for Arenas, Schools and XP.

**Cost:**
- **New inputs:** 4 per hero (luck, morale, and their temporary parts), which bumps the schema to version 8.
- **Evals:** Φ goes to version 3, so campaign evals start a fresh comparison series.

The perf session has main until about 09:45. I'll start then unless you want different numbers.

[2026-10-30 10:01] AI: Your example fails for the reasons you give. The general lesson is what makes a good target for an inner layer:
- **Bounded and scale-free:** a probability, a fraction, a class, or a clipped log-ratio. Never gold.
- **Dense:** defined for most areas or heroes at most decisions, and cleanly masked where it isn't.
- **Mostly local:** predictable from the unit's own neighbourhood. A target that needs the whole board trains the trunk, not the block encoder.
- **Low noise:** a short horizon (next turn, +2 days) or a deterministic quantity.
- **Stationary if possible:** map facts and pathfinder results don't change as our policy changes; "where we'll go" does.

This should help a lot here. Right now the map encoder and the hero-view convolutions learn only from the policy gradient on the one tile or area chosen, plus 2–7-day share labels. That's very little, very noisy signal for a lot of parameters.

**Ideas, roughly in the order I'd try them:**

1. **Area crossing cost (map encoder, the 18×18 areas).**
   - **Labels are already in every decision:** the pathfinder's days from each of our heroes to all 648 areas (`travel_days`).
   - **Local target per area:** how many days it costs to enter it from its best neighbour (water, mountains, a guard, no road), plus a reachable bit.
   - **Why:** enemy reach is currently straight-line tile distance (`features.reach`), which ignores water and mountains. With a learned cost map, the model can tell an enemy two days away from one across a lake, and judge our towns' safety the same way.
   - Free, dense and deterministic.

2. **Hero fate (hero tokens, ours and the enemy heroes we can see).**
   - **Targets:**
     - still alive and with the same owner in the next day's ledger, and at +2 days;
     - army kept, as log(worth then / worth now) clipped to [−3, 1].
   - **Labels are already in the ledgers:** heroes by type, with their armies.
   - **Why:** this is the exact failure we see against Nullkiller2, heroes ending the day where they die on its turn.

3. **Threat map (areas and hero-view tiles).**
   - **Target per area:** did an enemy hero that could beat ours stand within a day's walk of it at our next turn. Scored 0 to 1, as the max over enemies of reach × sigmoid(strength ratio).
   - **Mostly local:** enemy towns, last-seen heroes and nearby roads carry most of it.
   - **Needs one ledger field:** hero positions. That's information we can't see, so it's used only as a target, never as an input.
   - **Why:** it would replace the hand-made danger feature, which only sees visible heroes.

4. **Object fate (hero-view tiles and map objects).**
   - **Target per visible pickup:** at +2 days it's still there, taken by us, or taken by a rival.
   - **Labels from our own later inputs:** the object disappears from what we see.
   - **Why:** it teaches which piles are contested and which are safe to leave for tomorrow.

5. **Fight outcome (the tile a fight starts on, with its hero).**
   - **Target:** win / retreat / lose, plus the share of army kept, for every fight that actually happened (dozens per game).
   - **Why:** it calibrates a learned replacement for the hand-made win-probability curve. The hero-view convolutions learn what a stack shown as "several Behemoths" really means.

6. **Hidden map content (map encoder, the 9×9 blocks).**
   - **Target per block:** which object classes and terrain are there, predicted for unrevealed blocks from the revealed ones.
   - **Why it's learnable:** random maps are very regular (a town with its mines and dwellings, guarded passes between zones), so this is local and stationary.
   - **Label options:** a one-time dump of the true map per game (target only). Or, with no hidden information at all, masked-object modelling: hide some visible objects and predict them from the rest.

7. **Area control (areas with mines, dwellings or towns).**
   - **Target:** the share of those that are ours, a rival's or nobody's at +7 days.
   - It shows where the game is being decided, but it's slow and depends on our own policy. I'd try it last.

**What I'd skip:**
- anything in gold per block (your point);
- "where will our hero be tomorrow", which just learns our own policy back and shifts as it changes;
- long horizons (+7 days or game end) for local units, which carry too much luck for a small latent.

**Wiring is as you describe:**
- **Latent and head:** each unit (area, block, hero, tile) gets a small latent. A tiny head (linear or one hidden layer) reads only that latent, and its output never reaches the policy.
- **Into the trunk:** the latent is concatenated into what feeds the trunk.
- **Losses:** each one is a cross-entropy or clipped regression with weight around 0.1, masked where undefined. Each is logged separately so we can see which ones are being learned and remove any that hurts.

**I'd start with 1, 2 and 3.** The first two need no new data; the third needs one ledger field.

**One question for you:** are hidden-information targets OK in your view (enemy positions we can't see, the true map)? They never become inputs. The model learns to guess them from what a human would see, which is also how a human player learns.

[2026-10-30 10:45] AI: **Your three area targets.**
- **Two problems with them.** All three are bounded and local; the trouble is what they measure.
  - Counted over what we've seen, (1) is a function of the inputs. The model can already compute it, so the extra loss teaches little.
  - Counted over the true map, all three become hidden-information targets. (2) is one by definition, since its denominator is what we haven't seen.
- **The memorization risk is real but containable.** Every game is a fresh random map, so nothing memorized helps later. The danger is one map's answer, repeated over hundreds of its decisions, dominating the gradient.
  - Weighting the auxiliary loss per game rather than per decision fixes that: each game gets the same total weight, spread over its positions. That gives the "one position per game" effect without throwing data away.
  - The same loss on held-out games tells us if it memorizes anyway.
- **Map-centric vs hero-centric:** agreed. Area latents are only read through a hero: MapReader attends by direction and distance, and TRAVEL scores hero × area. So they're hero-relative in use, but a hero-centric target lands right where the decision is made. That's why I'd start with the fight head.

## The fight head

**What it predicts.** For every place where one of our actions can start a battle, it predicts two things:
- the battle's score by the battle reward's own formula in `reward.py`: what the enemy lost minus what we lost, over both sides' starting assets, from −1 to 1;
- P(win).

Both are bounded, scale-free and in the battle model's units.

**Where battles start.** For now, MOVE tiles with something to fight: a wandering monster or its zone of control, an enemy hero, a town with a garrison, a creature bank. `tile_features` already marks these tiles as `fights`. Later it could also cover a dialog's "fight" option, TRAVEL paths, and enemy attacks on us.

**Network change.** Yes, exactly your idea: one feature per battle-starting action, connected only to that action.
- **Inputs, per candidate tile only (a handful per window):**
  - our hero's own features, taken before the transformer layers: army, primary skills, secondary skills, spells, artifacts, mana;
  - what we'd fight, as we see it: the stack's creature and typical count for a monster or its zone, the enemy hero's or town's token, or a bank's guards;
  - the hand-made fight features: log strength ratio, and the prior's win and loss estimates;
  - the tile's convolution features, since the terrain there is the battlefield.
- **Output:** a small MLP gives a P(win) logit and a tanh score.
- **How it feeds the policy:** two new MOVE features on that tile, zero everywhere else. ActionScore learns their weights starting from 0.
  - The features are **detached**: the policy reads the prediction but can't bend it, so only real outcomes train the head.

```python
win_logit, score = self.fight(hero[pick], enemy[pick], handmade[pick])  # pick: fight tiles only
move_features[pick, FIGHT] = torch.stack([win_logit.sigmoid(), score], -1).detach()
# loss, at decisions that started a battle, on the chosen tile:
aux = bce(win_logit[started], won) + huber(score[started], realized_score)
```

- **Later, once it is better calibrated than the hand-made curve:** it replaces `win_chance(ratio)` and `expected_loss` in the MOVE prior and in the danger feature. The two would be blended by measured calibration, the way the value heads are by trust.

**Label.**
- **C++ capture:** `AlphaMapAI::battleStart` and `battleEnd` already fire for our battles; today they only track status.
  - At the start, record both sides' assets at the battle reward's prices: armies, hero level value, war machines, mana.
  - At the end, the outcome and casualties give the score by the same formula.
- **Transport:** it's sent like the ledger, keyed to the decision that started the battle: our last decision before it, either the MOVE or the dialog answer.
- **Python side:** `labels.py` attaches the score to that decision. The loss covers only decisions that started a battle, at the chosen tile, with weight around 0.2, averaged over battles. I'd log it with a calibration table (predicted vs realized, by bins).

**Data and bias.**
- **Volume:** every fight our heroes start counts, which is dozens per game and thousands per hour across the actors.
- **Selection:** we only see outcomes for fights we chose. But the choice was made on the same inputs the head sees (the policy can't see true counts either), so the outcome given those inputs isn't biased. The head just sees few hopeless fights; sampling at temperature 1 supplies some.

**The bigger version.** Make the core a matchup model on structured armies: our stacks plus hero against their stacks as seen.
- **More training data:** it can train on every battle we have, including the generated ones. Their records hold both armies and the reward. The enemy's true count becomes the quantity label the map would have shown ("few", "several", …).
- **Reuse:** it can then score TRAVEL's guards and the enemy heroes' threat, P(they beat us). That would replace the hand-made sigmoid of the strength ratio.

**Two choices for you:**
- **Score format:** a single mean or a few bins. I'd start with P(win) plus the mean.
- **Enemy-started battles:** whether battles enemies start against us should train it too. That would make the same head our danger model.

[2026-10-30 10:58] AI: I think it's a good idea. Auxiliary heads whose hidden state feeds forward (not their outputs) are a standard, proven way to give encoders dense, low-noise gradients, and ours are starved of exactly that. One change matters most: **a target that depends on the action has to be predicted per action, not per state.**

**Name:** "foresight heads". They look one step ahead; we train them but don't trust their outputs directly.

**Your five targets:**

1. **End-of-turn value change: good, and the label is free.**
   - Φ in the graph equals the ledger's to the gold, so Φ at our END decision minus Φ now is exact for every decision.
   - **Two forms:** log(Φ_end / Φ_now) for the % change, and the change in our share (rivals only move during our turn when we fight them).
   - **A hero-centric version:** the part of that change made by each hero's own actions today. That's free too, since every decision says which hero acted.
   - **One flag:** this is within-day. As an inner-layer target it doesn't touch the credit, so I think it's inside your rule, but you should know.
2. **Battle score if a battle happens: good, per candidate battle tile, as designed above.** It's the only target here that needs new data (the battle hook).
3. **Value change from the next action: good, but only per action.**
   - **Per state, it's wrong:** "the change from the next action" is the average over our own policy's choices, so it mostly learns our policy back.
   - **Per action, it's right:** score each MOVE tile, each HIRE slot, each BUILD entry and so on with its own immediate ΔΦ. That gives a learned, per-hero, per-context version of what the hand-made tile prior guesses.
   - **Label:** free (Φ before and after), for the action actually taken. Selection is on the same inputs the head sees, so the label isn't biased.
   - **Shape:** most immediate changes are exactly 0 (buying at list price is neutral). So predict P(nonzero) plus a signed log size, rather than one regression.
4. **Resources: worth doing.** Our economy collapsed against Nullkiller2, gold stuck at 400–2,000.
   - **Target:** per resource, tomorrow's stock against today's, as log((r' + c) / (r + c)) with c about a day's income.
   - **Or a classification:** will we be short of resources for the next building.
   - The label is free, from the next day's inputs.
5. **Widest value change: not labelable as I read it.** If it means the best immediate gain any legal action could get, we only ever see the action actually taken. It can still be a derived feature: the max of (3)'s per-action predictions over the legal actions, like the "offers" summary the type head already reads. If you meant something else, tell me.

**Wiring:**
- **Hidden size:** 8–16 per head, concatenated into the hero, tile or global features, with at least one nonlinear layer before anything that changes the policy. Your design is fine.
- **No detach on the hidden states.** They're representation; the auxiliary loss keeps them meaningful. Any scalar prediction fed in directly as a feature would be detached.
- **Losses:** bounded targets, each weighted about 0.1–0.3 and logged separately, so we can see which ones are learned and remove any that hurts.
- **Map-specific targets:** weight per game, not per decision.

**Order of work:** do the labels and losses first, because they don't depend on the architecture. That's `labels.py`, the records, and one C++ hook for battles. Then attach the heads to the current model as a cheap test of whether they're learnable on held-out games. The new architecture then keeps them.

[2026-10-30 11:39] AI: The short version:
- **The schema says what every input is**, and one encoder turns any declared input into normalized vectors.
- **Domain knowledge is computed first** and enters through the same encoders.
- **The trunk runs in two stages** around the foresight heads.
- **The priors stay where they are**, added to the logits.

## The forward

```python
def forward(self, x):
    known = self.domain_knowledge(x)            # Φ, fights, tile values, danger, Nullkiller2's habits: from the raw inputs
    state = self.encode(x, known)               # every input and every known feature -> normalized tokens and grids
    state = self.think(state)                   # the window and map CNNs, then the trunk: the dense state
    foresight = self.foresee(state)             # foresight heads: small hidden states, and predictions for the losses
    state = self.think_again(state, foresight)  # their hidden states joined in, more layers
    return self.decide(state, known), foresight # each action table: learned logits + its domain prior
```

`state` is one small object (global, heroes, towns, options, window tiles, map areas), so every block takes and returns the same thing. Sizes, activations, and transformer vs MLP inside `think` are left to the hyperparameter search. The foresight heads branch off the shared trunk, not off a separate path from the raw inputs. That way their losses shape the encoders the policy uses, which is the point of having them.

## Step 2: a sane way to process inputs

Today each call site in `model.py` picks its own transform and constants: `scales(x, (5, 20, 80))` in one place, `(500, 2000, 8000)` in another. The same quantity is scaled differently in different places. Some inputs never reach a learned layer at all: `h_luck` and `h_morale` only feed Φ, and the learned part of TRAVEL never sees `travel_days`. Nothing checks for either problem.

The fix is to make it declarative:

1. **Each input declares its kind and unit in the schema**, one line each, next to its doc. For example: `_i("h_mana", (H,), "mana", unit="mana")`, `_m("t_built", ..., kind="bits")`, `_i("h_pos", ..., kind="position")`.
2. **One encoder per kind**, with shared code and separate weights per input:

   | Kind | Encoding |
   |---|---|
   | category (ids) | embedding; −1 becomes a zero vector |
   | amount (counts, gold, mana, movement, days, tiles, experience) | log1p(x/s), x/(x+s/4), x/(x+s), x/(x+4s), x>0, then a linear layer; s is the unit's scale |
   | signed amount (gains, changes) | symlog(x/s), tanh(x/s), then a linear layer |
   | level (skill levels, fort, luck, morale, day of week) | one-hot, then a linear layer |
   | flag, bits (buildings, spells, tile flags) | 0/1, then a linear layer |
   | position | relative to the hero or town reading it: direction and distance in tiles |
   | set (army stacks, artifacts, options) | each element encoded by its own fields, then pooled (sum and max) |

3. **About ten unit scales, set by hand and documented.** Examples: gold 1,000, creatures 20, movement 1,500, mana 50, experience 5,000, days 3, tiles 10. The four-scale bank around each covers three orders of magnitude, so a scale only needs to be roughly right. You decide an input's unit once, with no per-feature thinking.
4. **A token is the sum of its fields' encodings, then a LayerNorm.** Tiles and map blocks are built the same way, then go through their CNN.
5. **Two tests keep it sane:** every schema input is consumed by some encoder, and every encoded value stays within a few units over the input's whole range.

Special cases go through domain knowledge first, then the same encoders. A monster's count, for example, is a quantity label ("few", "several"…). It enters both as a category and, via `typical_counts`, as an amount of creatures.

The window CNN needs a real receptive field. Today it is two 3×3 layers, so a tile sees only the 5×5 around it and nothing of the route from the hero. A few residual blocks with a downsample and upsample would fix that.

## Domain knowledge goes in first, as inputs

Compute it from the raw inputs before anything learned, as `make_custom_features` does now. Then feed it through the same encoders as extra fields of the token it describes:
- Φ parts go to the global token.
- Strength, worth and level gain go to each hero.
- Object gold, fight return, P(win) and danger go to each tile.
- Travel value goes to each area.

Early is better than concatenating late. With residual layers an early field stays in the stream to the end anyway, and the layers in between can combine it with everything else. The priors stay additive on the logits, in `decide`.

## Foresight heads

Each head sits where a decision is made. It produces a small hidden state (8–16 values) that is joined back into its token, plus predictions for the loss:

| Head | Where | Targets |
|---|---|---|
| move | every legal MOVE tile (label at the chosen one) | whether its consequences include a battle; that battle's score, by the battle reward's formula; the change in each Φ part (resources, army, heroes, artifacts, mana, explored) |
| answer | every option of a question | the same three |
| hero | each of our heroes | its share of today's remaining Φ change; alive and still ours tomorrow |
| turn | global | Φ change to the end of our turn, as a % and as our share's change; each resource tomorrow vs today |

**The consequence window runs from a turn decision to our next turn decision**, including every question and battle in between.
- **Your point about deciding after seeing what's there:** the chest's gold-or-experience choice, the University's skill, and the guarded dwelling we agree to attack all land in that MOVE's window.

**Losses:**
- **Value changes:** symlog targets, regressed as two-hot over bins. This is DreamerV3's recipe, robust to heavy tails and to the many exact zeros.
- **Yes/no targets:** BCE.
- **Weights and logging:** each head weighted 0.1–0.3 and logged separately.
- **Not exported:** the predictions never reach the AI, which only gets the policy and value outputs.

3. **The new model in its own file, trained from scratch.** Today's checkpoint can't be migrated to it. Keep the current model for comparison, and run the size search once the new one trains.

[2026-10-30 12:11] AI: Three ideas carry this design.

1. **One map at tile resolution, shared by everyone.** All our maps are 36×36 with two levels, 2,592 tiles. Today each hero gets its own 33×33 window, which is nearly the whole level again for every hero. One grid costs less, and every tile gets the same CNN.
2. **Shared encoders, so heroes, towns and tiles live in one space.** The same function turns any hero into a vector, whether ours, an enemy's or one for hire. Likewise any army: a hero's, a garrison, a monster, a bank's guards. Heroes and towns are stamped onto their tiles, and heroes read the tiles through attention.
3. **A logit is a match, not a forward pass.** It is the actor's score, plus the actor's query dotted with the target's key, plus a small network over legal pairs only, plus the domain prior. One softmax covers every legal action, so a MOVE, a BUILD and END are scored on one scale.

## The forward

```python
def forward(self, x):
    known = self.domain_knowledge(x)                    # features.py as now: Φ, fights, tile values, danger, the priors
    state = self.encode(x)                              # raw inputs only -> entity vectors and the tile grid
    state = self.join(state, known)                     # known features concatenated onto what they describe
    state = self.see(state)                             # entities onto their tiles, the map CNN, heroes and towns read the tiles
    state = self.think(state)                           # transformer over the entity tokens
    foresight = self.foresee(state)                     # foresight hidden states, and predictions for the losses
    state = self.think_again(state, foresight, known)   # foresight and known joined again, more layers
    return self.decide(state, known), foresight         # logits by matching, plus the domain priors
```

## `encode`: the functions it calls

| Function | Takes | Gives |
|---|---|---|
| `encode_army` | stacks (creature, plus count or the quantity label) | an army vector, plus per-stack vectors for ARMY and UPGRADE |
| `encode_hero` | type, class, level, primary and secondary skills, spells, artifacts, mana, movement, luck and morale, its army | one hero vector. The same function serves ours, the enemies' (unknown fields left empty) and the tavern's |
| `encode_town` | faction, buildings, fort, garrison, creatures for hire by level | a town vector, plus level vectors for RECRUIT |
| `encode_object` | type, subtype, owner, flags, guards | an object vector |
| `encode_tiles` | terrain, road, flags, the object on the tile | the tile grid, [2, 36, 36, c] |
| `encode_global`, `encode_options` | day, resources, income, the question and its options | tokens |

Every raw field goes through the typed encoders from before: each input's kind and unit are declared in the schema. Because the encoders are shared, a tavern hero and our main hero are directly comparable.

## `see`: tiles and entities

- **Stamp.** Each hero's and town's vector is projected and added onto its tile. The grid then knows that *this* strong enemy hero stands here, not just "a hero", and the CNN carries that outward. This answers your point that heroes and towns are not all equal.
- **Map CNN.** A U-Net over the grid, going 36 → 18 → 9 → 18 → 36, so each tile sees the route to it and what lies a day or two around it. The 18×18 level doubles as TRAVEL's areas.
- **Read.** Each of our heroes attends over the tiles, with its own reach added to the keys: the pathfinder's turns and movement left, for that hero, on that tile. Its vector ends up holding things like "gold pile 4 tiles away, weak guards on the mine, an enemy 2 days out". Towns read the tiles around them the same way.

## `decide`: how a logit is made

`logit(actor, target) = act_now(actor) + query(actor) · key(target | actor) + pairnet(actor, target) + prior`

- **MOVE.**
  - The actor is a hero: its act-now score and its query come from its vector after the trunk.
  - The key is the tile's vector plus that hero's reach to the tile.
  - One batched matmul scores every hero × tile.
  - The pair network sees each pair's foresight hidden state and its known features (gold, P(win), danger). It runs only on legal pairs, a few hundred per hero.
- **The other tables**, all as actor × target:

  | Action | Actor | Target |
  |---|---|---|
  | TRAVEL | hero | 18×18 area |
  | BUILD | town | building |
  | RECRUIT | town | level (× amount, destination) |
  | HIRE | town | tavern hero, in the same hero space |
  | ARMY | stack | holder |
  | CAST, BUY | hero | spell or item |
  | Questions | the global token plus the hero being asked | option |

- **One softmax over every legal action.** A type's probability is the logsumexp of its entries. END competes directly with the best MOVE, so the hand-made couplings ("value in reach holds END back") become unnecessary. The AI still samples a type, then an entry within it.

That's how it knows which hero moves. The joint softmax over hero × tile picks the hero. Hero A's vector has read its own tiles (the pile in reach, nothing threatening) and, through the trunk, hero B's (B is closer to it). So A's act-now score and its query against the pile's key carry "B should take it".

## `foresee` and `think_again`

Foresight hidden states live where the decisions are:
- **per legal (hero, tile) pair:** was there a battle, its score, and each Φ part's change;
- **per option;**
- **per hero;**
- **globally.**

They are joined, with the known features again, into the pair network and the entity vectors. That late path is how a single number like P(win) reaches the logit without being swallowed.

## What it costs

- **Contract changes:**
  - In: a map grid of tile fields [2, 36, 36] and each hero's reach on it.
  - Out: the eight windows and the 8,192-object list.
  - MOVE indexes map tiles instead of window cells. The C++ encoder changes; the type-then-entry sampling doesn't.
- **Domain knowledge:** `features.py` stays. Its tile functions move from windows to the map grid.
- **Training:** starts from scratch, since none of today's weights fit.

**Two decisions for you:**
1. **Fix the grid at 36×36×2 while maps are small.** I recommend it. Bigger maps would later need a crop around our heroes, or the windows back.
2. **Use one softmax over all actions** instead of the type head plus couplings. I recommend this too.

## Campaign model

### The forward

```python
def forward(self, x):
    known = self.domain_knowledge(x)                    # facts from the raw inputs: Φ, fights, values, danger, reference sizes, priors
    state = self.encode(x)                              # raw inputs only -> entity vectors and the tile grid
    state = self.take_sides(state)                      # every vector transformed by who owns it: ours, nobody's, which rival's
    state = self.join(state, known)                     # known facts concatenated onto what they describe
    state = self.see(state)                             # entities onto their tiles, the map CNN, heroes and towns read the tiles
    state = self.think(state)                           # transformer over entity and player tokens
    foresight = self.foresee(state)                     # foresight hidden states, and predictions for the losses
    state = self.think_again(state, foresight, known)   # foresight and known joined again, more layers
    return self.decide(state, known), foresight         # every logit a match, plus its prior; one softmax
```

Each block calls many small functions, listed below. The forward names only the blocks.

### 1. `domain_knowledge`: facts and references

These are today's functions from `features.py`:
- **Φ parts;** army strength and worth;
- **hero worth** and level gains;
- **town strength,** value and danger;
- **object worth** and guard strength;
- **win chance,** expected loss and fight return;
- **exploration;** the travel prior;
- **Nullkiller2's habits;** hire gains.

The tile functions move off the windows: the parts that don't depend on the hero go per map tile, the hero-dependent parts go per (hero, tile) pair.

New: **reference sizes**, which are what "large" means right now:
- our Φ;
- our strongest hero's army and our total army;
- the strongest rival army we can see;
- our daily income;
- each hero's daily movement;
- the week number.

### 2. `encode`: raw inputs only

| Function | Gives |
|---|---|
| `encode_army` | stacks → per-stack vectors and one army vector. The same function serves heroes, garrisons, monsters, bank guards, tavern heroes and the other army in an exchange |
| `encode_hero` | one vector per hero, the same function for ours, the rivals' (unknown fields left empty) and the tavern's |
| `encode_town` | a town vector, plus level vectors for RECRUIT |
| `encode_object` | an object vector |
| `encode_tiles` | the tile grid at the map's real size: terrain, road, flags, revealed or not, the object on the tile |
| `encode_global`, `encode_options` | tokens |

Every field goes through the typed encoders: its kind and unit are declared in the schema.
- **Amounts:** absolute, through the bank of scales around their unit.
- **Day of the week:** an embedding.
- **Week number:** log-scaled and saturating.
- **Ownership:** encode doesn't use it. The next block does.

### 3. `take_sides`: ownership transforms everything

- **Relation to us.** Every entity and tile gets one: ours, nobody's, or a rival's. Each relation has its own learned affine transform per channel, starting at +1 for ours and nobody's and −1 for rivals. That's the battle model's signed half, generalized.
- **Which rival.** Each rival also adds its identity embedding, by turn order relative to us. Two rivals are both "against us" but are not the same.
- **Player tokens.** There's one per player, ours and each rival's we know of, pooled from their entities. "Which rival is the threat" becomes explicit, and the value heads read ours against theirs.
- **Attention pair bias.** The trunk's attention gets a learned bias per relation of the pair: same owner, us vs a rival, rival vs the same rival, rival vs another rival, anything vs nobody.

### 4. Scale relative to the situation

Log scales alone can't say whether an army is large. That's relative to the week and to the whole board, so every amount enters twice:
- **absolutely,** from `encode`;
- **relatively,** as `join` adds it from the references: a clipped log ratio against its unit's reference.

| Amount | Relative to |
|---|---|
| armies | our main army, our total army, our Φ, the strongest rival army seen |
| resources | days of our income, the next building's cost |
| movement | the hero's daily movement |
| distances | days of walking |
| mana | casts of the hero's dearest spell |
| counts on the map | the map's size |

References have floors (our Φ is at least 1,000), so ratios stay bounded early in a game. Because the references grow with the weeks, "large" moves with the game.

### 5. `see`: the map at tile resolution, any size

- **One grid per level at the map's real size,** shared by every hero.
  - Hidden tiles carry only an "unrevealed" flag.
  - Off-map cells are masked after every layer.
  - The ONNX model takes height and width as dynamic axes. Records carry the map size, and batches group decisions by size or pad with the mask.
- **Stamping.** Each hero's and town's vector, after ownership, is added onto its tile. The grid knows that this strong rival hero stands here.
- **U-Net.** Strides of 2 and back, so each tile sees the route to it and a day or two around it.
  - Its coarser levels, pooled by area index into today's fixed 18×18 areas per level, are TRAVEL's targets, so TRAVEL's contract doesn't change.
- **Reading.** Each of our heroes attends over the tiles, with its own reach added to the keys. Towns read the tiles around them the same way.
- **Per-hero reach stays a fixed 33×33 window.** That's today's `w_turns` and `w_move_left`, scattered onto the grid by position. Records stay small on big maps, and MOVE keeps its window-relative indexing.
- **Cost.**
  - A 36×36 map has 2,592 tiles, less than today's windows (one nearly full level per hero).
  - On a 144×144 map the AI would compute the static part (terrain, objects) once per turn as a separate graph and reuse it. That can wait until we play big maps.

### 6. `think`

A transformer over global, player, hero, town, option, tavern-hero and other-army tokens. It uses the relation biases plus the existing tile-offset bias between placed tokens.

### 7. `foresee` and `think_again`

Foresight heads, each a hidden state of 8–16 joined back where it was computed:

| Head | Where | Targets |
|---|---|---|
| move | every legal (hero, tile) pair | battle or not; its score by the battle reward's formula; the change in each Φ part, over the consequence window |
| answer | every option of a question | the same |
| hero | each of our heroes | its share of today's remaining Φ change; alive and ours tomorrow |
| turn | global | Φ change to the end of our turn, and our share's change; each resource tomorrow vs today |

- **The consequence window** runs from a turn decision to our next turn decision, including the questions and battles in between.
- **Labels** are free from the records, except the battle score, which needs the `battleStart`/`battleEnd` hook.
- **Losses:** symlog two-hot regression and BCE, weight 0.1–0.3 each, never exported to the AI.
- **`think_again`** concatenates the foresight hidden states and the known facts again, onto entities and onto (hero, tile) pairs, then runs more layers. That late path is how a single number like P(win) reaches a logit without being swallowed.

### 8. `decide`: every logit a match, one softmax

`logit = act_now(actor) + query(actor) · key(target | actor) + pairnet(actor, target, its foresight, its known facts) + prior`

| Type | Actor × target |
|---|---|
| MOVE | hero × its window's tiles (the key is the tile's map vector plus the hero's reach) |
| TRAVEL | hero × area |
| BUILD | town × building |
| RECRUIT | town × level × amount × destination |
| HIRE | town × tavern hero |
| ARMY | stack × holder × amount |
| UPGRADE | holder × stack |
| TRADE | resource × resource × amount |
| CAST, BUY | hero × spell or item |
| questions | (global + the hero asked) × option |
| END | the global token alone |

- **Dot products** for the whole table are batched matmuls.
- **The pair network** runs only on legal entries, a few thousand at most per decision. Compute is fine.
- **One softmax over all legal actions:**
  - a type's log-probability is the logsumexp of its entries, so END competes directly with the best MOVE;
  - the hand-made couplings and the separate type head go away;
  - each type's act-now bias absorbs the difference in table sizes.
- **Unchanged:** the AI still samples a type, then an entry.

### 9. Values

V2, V5, V7, growth and V_end read the global token and the player tokens: our share against each rival's.

### Contract changes

- **Added:** the tile grid at the map's size.
- **Removed:** the per-window terrain and object fields, and the 8,192-object list (objects live on their tiles).
- **Kept:** the windows, for reach and MOVE only. TRAVEL and the other tables don't change.
- **Training:** from scratch.

## Battle model

It already follows most of these principles, and these parts stay:
- **the signed half:** with exactly two sides, a sign flip is right;
- **pointer logits;**
- **the engine's own value for every attack and spell,** played on a copy of the battle;
- **Lanchester strength shares** going straight to the value and type heads.

What I'd change:

1. **Foresight on the response, not on our own action.** The engine already computes what our action does exactly. What the model has to guess is what happens before our next decision. Targets:
   - each of our units: dies before its next turn; health lost by then;
   - each enemy unit: damage it deals before our next decision, and whom it attacks (a pointer over our units);
   - each hex: whether an enemy can reach it;
   - the chosen action: the round score's change until our next decision.

   The labels are free from consecutive decisions in the battle records and the event history they already carry.
2. **One softmax over all actions.** Joint over type × target × attack hex × second target, replacing the type head plus the summed "best follow-up" and escape couplings. Engine values and priors stay added per entry. That's up to about 15,000 entries, mostly masked, so it's cheap.
3. **The same typed encoders and the same late join of known facts.** Each choice's engine value enters its logit's last layer, which extends what the strength shares already do for the value head.
4. **Optional link to the campaign.** The two models can share the creature and ability encoders. The campaign's fight head can then be trained against the battle model's own value at the start of each battle.
5. **Size.** Width and depth (64 × 2 layers now) go to the hyperparameter search, as for the campaign.

## Decisions for you

1. **Per-hero reach and MOVE stay in fixed 33×33 windows on top of the shared variable-size map.** This keeps records small and MOVE's contract stable. I recommend it.
2. **Rivals are identified by turn order relative to us.** The alternative is ordering by strength rank, which changes during a game. Turn order is what I'd use.
3. **The battle model's change can be done separately.** Items 1–3 are independent of the campaign rewrite, and item 1 alone should help the most.

**Battle model: yes, it already makes every logit a projection.** For each kind of choice, a query built from the decision's context is dotted with a key from each unit's or hex's token. On top of that come a learned score of the engine's own features for that choice and the value prior. Here's what I'd change:

1. **The context is a bottleneck.** All seven queries are linear maps of one context vector. That vector squeezes the battle, the acting unit, our hero, the mean unit and the strength shares (276 numbers) through a 32-wide hidden layer. Every choice the unit makes depends mostly on which unit is acting, so I'd give each query a direct term from the acting unit's own token, and widen the context.
2. **One softmax over all actions.** Today each table normalizes separately, and a type's logit adds the *max* of its children (`best_of`). The right quantity is a logsumexp: with the max, a type with one great target scores the same as one with five equally great ones. The fix:
   - Score each full entry (type, then target, then attack hex or second target) as a sum along that path.
   - Normalize once. The type's probability becomes the logsumexp of its entries.
   - Wait, defend, retreat and surrender become entries scored by their own features, such as the escapes' exact reward.
   - The separate type MLP and its strength and escape couplings go away. The AI still samples a type, then an entry.
3. **Foresight on the enemy's response, not on our own action.** The engine already computes exactly what our attack does, on a copy of the battle. What the model has to guess is what happens before our next decision:
   - **Each enemy unit:** the damage it deals before our next turn, and which of our units it hits. This joins its key, so killing whatever is about to hurt us most stands out.
   - **Each of our units:** whether it dies before its next turn, and how much health it loses. This joins its token, so the model sees who needs protecting.
   - **Each hex:** whether an enemy can reach it. This joins the hex key, so the model sees where it's safe to stand.
   - **The chosen action:** the round score's change until our next decision. This joins that choice's score.

   The labels come free from consecutive decisions in the battle records and the event history between them.
4. **Joining known facts late: mostly there already.** Engine features already reach each choice through its own feature score, and the strength shares already go straight to the value and type heads. I'd keep both and add the foresight hidden states to the same path.
5. **Size.** Width 64, 2 layers and that 32-wide context go into the size search.

Items 2 and 3 are independent of the campaign rewrite. Item 3 should help the most, since the response is exactly where the battle model is guessing today.

## What I did since your last message

**Battle model** (commit `f3e5b1d`):
- **Foresight heads:** they predict the enemy's reply before our next decision — which of our units die, the health they lose, the damage each unit deals, and which hexes an enemy stands on. The labels come free from consecutive decisions in the battle records.
- **Wider context layer:** from 32 to 128 units. It was squeezing 276 inputs through 32 for every choice.
- **Acting unit in every query:** each choice's query now reads the acting unit directly.
- **No retraining needed:** every new part starts at zero, so joint2's checkpoint loads with identical outputs (to 4e-6). battle3's first eval confirmed it: **+0.090 against BattleAI** (joint2's level) and **+0.092 against MMAI**.
- **Gradient health:** logged every 5 updates — how much gradient the trunk gets from the foresight loss versus the main loss, whether they conflict, and which parameters get none.
- **Deferred: one softmax over all actions for the battle model.** It would change the trained policy's behaviour, and the current approximation isn't causing a known failure.

**Campaign v2** (commit `05914d0`, switched on by `campaign.model_architecture=v2`):
- **Built as designed:** raw-input encoders, ownership transforms, a U-Net over the whole map, heroes reading the tiles, foresight heads, every logit an actor-against-target match, one softmax over all actions.
- **Trained from scratch** in the next run, since nothing of v1's weights fits.
- **Tests:** all 274 pass. The new ones check that the ONNX export matches torch to 2e-6 and that every block receives gradient once training starts. A smoke game with one update also worked.
- **Cost:** 18.5 ms per decision for inference (v1: 9 ms) and 1.7× v1's training cost per decision.

**C++ (schema 9):**
- The AI now sends a full-map tile grid. In real games it matched every hero's view on all 260k tiles compared.
- It also sends a record of every battle, keyed to the decision that led to it. These are the labels for the fight foresight.

**Smaller items:**
- A fog fix in the map AI, from the other session's finding: VCMI was logging an error for every fogged tile asked about, costing about 11% of a campaign client's CPU.
- The battle trainer now builds its per-update features in place instead of concatenating chunks, which doubled the GPU peak.
- I merged the other session's work: battle clients use 18% less CPU per decision with identical outputs, and a memory setting stops the GPU caches from thrashing.

**One finding:** joint2's trained campaign model fought only 1–3 battles in 21 days of a 3-player game. That avoidance of fights is likely part of why it loses to Nullkiller2.

## What I changed

Four things I'd call predictable failures, one change to the training signal, and one labelling fix.

1. **The action-type score was wrong.** I had set a type's score to the log-mean-exp of its table's entries. Among 300 legal tiles, a few good ones barely moved the mean, so MOVE could never beat END on their account; the model would have had to learn to push 300 worthless tiles down one by one. Now a type is as good as its best option: its score is its bias, what its domain prior offers (MOVE's best tile value as a logit, so value in reach holds END back, as in v1), and the best learned entry.
2. **Zero starts.** Every head's last layer now starts at zero, so the first policy is exactly the hand-made priors. Before, random output layers added noise of about ±0.5 logits to priors of 2–4.
3. **Fixed shapes on the GPU.** The window tensors varied in size with the number of heroes in a minibatch. Apple's GPU keeps a compiled graph per shape, about 100 MB each; v1 had hit this and padded. v2 now stays padded through the pairs and the foresight.
4. **A third of the training games are against Nullkiller2** (`campaign.nullkiller_share`), at a difficulty drawn from (1, 1, 2). Self-play never faced its aggression: joint2's eval against it stayed at 0.14 of parity while every self-play measure improved. What only Nullkiller2 punishes, self-play cannot teach. A smoke game with us in one seat and it in two ran clean.
5. **Foresight labels** are computed on every record as sent, before unusable decisions are dropped, because the battle records point at record serials.

Reviewed and left as they are: the labels and credit (7-day horizon with TD steps, the V_end credit), the eval (v1's games took at most 127 s against a 600 s limit, so v2's 2× slower inference fits), and the hyperparameters. All 274 tests pass. Committed as `1f7db1c`, local.

## The prediction

The metric is `eval/campaign`: our share of all empires' value at day 56 against Nullkiller2, times the number of players. 1.0 is parity with the average player; joint2's v1 reached about 0.14 after days of training.

- **After 12 hours: 0.25–0.5.** Day-56 parity in 12 hours is not realistic from scratch: the credit is the limit. The share labels change once a day, so all of a day's decisions get the same push, and the learner sees about 2M decisions in 12 h. The foresight heads sharpen the representation, but they don't give per-action credit.
- **After 48 hours: 0.5–0.9**, if the NK2 games teach defence.
- **The sign to watch at 12 h:** below 0.2 means the credit assignment is the limit, not the model, and the next change should be per-action credit, with the foresight predictions as a baseline. Above 0.5 means the model was the limit and more training is the answer.

**To start the run:**
```
PYTORCH_MPS_LOW_WATERMARK_RATIO=0.2 .venv/bin/python -m campaign_model.joint --run joint5 --hours 12 --battle-from runtime/saved/battle_battle3_05829.pt --set campaign.model_architecture=v2 campaign.model_cell_dim=16 campaign.games=4 campaign.passes=1 generated_actors=6
```
